"正如其名，歌舞伎舞蹈是歌舞伎的一个流派，指兼具戏剧元素的舞蹈。听到歌舞伎，很多人首先想到的或许是身着和服、留着发髻、佩戴打挂及梳子、发簪的形象。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "歌舞伎与马戏团，这两个看似风马牛不相及的事物，究竟是如何交织在一起的呢？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随着幕末开港，西方的物品、人物以及文化开始全面传入日本。马戏团也是作为西方的新兴演艺来到日本的事物之一。据记载，元治元年（1864年）横滨就曾有过马戏团演出。随后在明治4年（1871年），法国人苏里（Soulier）在如今的靖国神社境内举办了马戏演出。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "日本原本就有一种名为“曲马”的传统演艺，即展示骑马站在围棋盘上、骑马弹三味线等各种绝技。马戏也正是在此基础上，作为“西洋曲马”被人们所接受。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "text": "明治19年（1886年）7月，据记载作为日本迎来的第3个马戏团，是由意大利人朱塞佩·查利涅（Giuseppe Chiarini）率领的马戏团。这个环游世界的剧团在横滨赢得声誉后，开始在东京秋叶原演出。在当时因防火而成为空地的这片场地上，搭建了环绕圆形马场、观众席四周并用帐篷覆盖的巨型表演场——这也是如今人们熟悉的模样。在其中，上演了在飞奔的马背上进行杂技，以及利用大象、猴子、老虎惊险刺激的节目。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/5ea7d734ef9891b4bad4db2a405bb2ee.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "“伊太利亜国チヤリネ世界第一大曲馬遊覧之図”", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "查利涅的马戏团被报纸形容为“空前绝后的大曲马”并获得极大好评，演出场场爆满。11月，剧团还受邀前往吹上御苑，在明治天皇面前展示了精湛技艺。《明治天皇纪》中记载了查利涅的技艺，称赞其“妙技逼神，颇有令宸目愉悦者”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": article_text:
昭和41年（1966年）の開場以来、伝統芸能の上演だけでなく、演劇・芸能関連の資料の収集と活用に努めてきた国立劇場。美術的に優れた名品から歴史的に貴重な資料まで、多岐にわたる所蔵資料から、担当者が「これを見て！」という一押しを紹介するのが、毎月末日に公開する美術展ナビ×国立劇場コラボ連載【芸能資料定期便】です。

今回は国立劇場の所蔵する浮世絵から、こちらの作品をご紹介します。

まず目に入るのは、中央で前足を上げた象。その前には、まさに象に指示を出している赤い服の男性と、気取ったポーズの青いドレスの女性が立っています。

右側には羽飾りをつけた馬と、馬に合図するモーニング姿の男性。そして赤い星柄に大きな襟の服を着て、白と赤の滑稽なメイクで笑う男性がいます。

絵の左側には杖をついて自分の写真を配っているらしき片足の男性、そしてハイカラな紙巻たばこを手に、椅子に座って彼らを眺める散切り頭の男性が描かれています。

芸をする動物たち、ユーモラスで華やかな衣裳、それを見物する人──そう、この浮世絵はサーカスの様子を描いています。眺めていると、観客をわくわくさせる楽しげな音楽まで聴こえてきそうです。

しかし、この作品は実際のサーカスを描いた絵ではありません。

この浮世絵は明治19年（1886年）11月に千歳座で上演された歌舞伎舞踊「 鳴響 茶利 音曲馬 」を題材に描かれたもの、つまり芝居絵です。三代歌川国貞としても知られる、四代歌川国政によって描かれました。

歌舞伎舞踊とは、その名の通り歌舞伎のジャンルの一つで、演劇の要素を持つ舞踊のことです。歌舞伎と聞けば、着物にちょんまげ、打掛や櫛・かんざしといった姿をまず思い浮かべる方が多いかもしれません。

そんな歌舞伎とサーカスという、一見するとかけ離れた両者は、どのようにして結びついたのでしょうか。

幕末の開港によって、日本にも本格的に西洋の物や人、そして文化がもたらされるようになりました。サーカスもまた、西洋の新しい芸能として日本にやってきたものの一つです。元治元年（1864年）には、横浜でサーカスの興行があったことが記録されています。次いで明治4年（1871年）フランス人のスリエによって、現在の靖国神社境内でサーカスの興行が行われました。

日本にはもともと、馬に乗って碁盤の上に立つ、馬に乗ったまま三味線を弾くなどさまざまな芸を披露する「曲馬」という芸能がありました。そこからサーカスも、「西洋曲馬」として受け入れられていきます。

明治19年（1886年）7月、記録上日本で3番目にやってきたのが、イタリア人のジュゼッペ・チャリネが率いるサーカス団です。世界各国を回ってきた一座は横浜で評判を取ったのち、東京・秋葉原で興行を始めます。当時防火のために空き地だったこの場所に、円形の馬場を囲うように客席を設け全体をテントで覆った、現在でもおなじみの巨大な演技場が建てられました。その内で、駆け巡る馬の上での曲芸や、象に猿、虎を使ったスリル満点の演芸が繰り広げられたのです。

新聞に「未曾有の大曲馬」とも記されたチャリネのサーカスは大評判を取り、興行は連日の大入りとなりました。11月には一座は吹上御苑に招かれ、明治天皇の前でもその芸を披露しています。『明治天皇紀』にはチャリネの芸について、「妙技神に迫り、頗る宸目を愉ばすものあり」と喜ばれたことが記されています。

明治期の歌舞伎の名優として知られる五代目尾上菊五郎も、10月の始めごろにチャリネの公演に足を運び、大いに刺激を受けました。そしてすぐさま河竹黙阿弥に注文して作った演目が、歌舞伎舞踊「鳴響茶利音曲馬」です。

凝り性で有名な菊五郎は、上演にあたってチャリネをはじめ一座の数人と面会して、サーカスについて教えを請いました。

チャリネはこの交流を快く受け入れたようで、親しく技芸を見せ、象などの動物の遣い方や道化師の顔の塗り方を菊五郎らに伝授しました。さらにこの演目の成功を祝して、各国の徽章のついた 縮緬 の大旗5流を彼らに贈りました。

公演では実寸大に作った馬や象の小道具の中へ役者が入って動くなど、工夫を凝らしてチャリネ直伝の芸が披露され、話題になりました。当時の記録には菊五郎の演じるチャリネについての評判も載っており「曲馬師チャリネの役からだが小さい 斗 り其他は恰好から歩きやう迄其人を見る如く」と、身体が小さいだけで本物と見間違えてしまいそうな完成度だったと記されています。

また菊五郎たちがサーカスを訪れたように、チャリネとその団員もたびたびこの芝居を見物に訪れました。客席は大いに盛り上がったことでしょう。

サーカスと歌舞伎という二つの芸の海を越えた出会いによって、歌舞伎舞踊「鳴響茶利音曲馬」は完成しました。今回ご紹介した浮世絵「鳴響茶利音曲馬」は、それぞれの芸を極めた彼らの交流の軌跡と、「人を楽しませたい」という心意気を今に伝える一枚といえるでしょう。

article_text:
Two Pierre-Auguste Renoir paintings stolen from a museum in the French Riviera last month have been recovered, local officials said. Six suspects were arrested.

The mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, where Renoir lived out his final days, described the news as “a source of immense joy and a great relief.” He added that the paintings were “part of our city’s history, our cultural heritage.”

Two thieves broke into the artist’s former home, the city’s Renoir Museum , early on September 8. They attempted to take four paintings before dropping two in the garden as they rushed to escape. The value of the two stolen works, Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Young Woman at the Well (1886), was reported at a combined $10 million. Both belong to the Musée d’Orsay in Paris and were on loan.

The Marseille public prosecutor’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how the Renoir paintings were recovered. A press conference that would have given more details about the recovery was canceled so as not to interfere with the ongoing investigation.

France’s culture minister, Catherine Pégard , commended “the efficiency and determination” of the investigators in a post on social media. She also praised the “swift response” of local police, “from the moment the alarm was triggered,” as “remarkable.”

France has suffered a spate of museum heists in recent years. The highest-profile one occurred at the Louvre in Paris last October. Investigators uncovered various security failings that left the institution vulnerable to the shock $102 million theft, and the Louvre announced a $92 million master security plan .

Though Renoir continues to divide opinion , the Impressionist just broke box-office records at the National Gallery in London, with the museum selling over 22,000 tickets for its “Renoir and Love” exhibition, which is on view through January 31.

article_text:
Amid the turmoil of mass student protests in the streets of Belgrade, two young people are bonded by a rash act of rebellion, despite their outwardly incompatible ideologies. The premise of Serbian writer-director Jelena Maksimović ‘s “ Until the Day Ends ” portends a tidy political parable — a sort of “why can’t we all get along” homily for an age, and particularly a generation, of vastly polarized beliefs. The execution, thankfully, is flintier and more complicated than that. The film’s teachings, if any, are ambiguous, and learned on the run: Maksimović’s first fiction feature is most memorable for its galloping formal restlessness, moving at the breathless pace of its characters as they evade authority and chase a glimmer of hope in their joint resistance.

Having made an impression on the docfest circuit with her two nonfiction features “Taurunum Boy” (2019) and “Homelands (2020), Maksimović brings a street-level, vérité -style grit to the lean narrative of “Until the Day Ends” that feels authentically keyed into the reality of current youth unrest in Eastern Europe. The film is set against a surge of real-life anti-government demonstrations in Serbia in early 2025, triggered by the tragic deaths of 16 people the previous year, following the collapse of a train station canopy in Novi Sad. But if the honest performances of a mostly non-professional ensemble contribute to a docudrama spirit, the filmmaker and her DP Paul Spengemann embrace an aesthetic of epic escapism, with roving, kinetic camerawork punctuated with enough bursting lens flare to make Janusz Kaminski blush.

It’s an attention-grabbing approach that promises bigger things from Maksimović, and is propelling the film some distance on the international festival circuit. A premiere last month in Venice’s Horizons program has since been followed with berths in Vienna, Hamburg and, now, the main competition in Tokyo.

The film opens on a virtuoso long take, roaming through the shadowed, disheveled hallways of a university building that, ahead of the revolution, has become something of a campsite for displaced, rebellious students; insurgent streaks of red disrupt the general gloom of the mise-en-scène. Through this faintly apocalyptic scene, we follow 20-year-old Lena (riveting newcomer Lena Trifunović), a firebrand student activist who is all in on the protests, unwavering in her anti-authoritarian conviction. That may earn her the admiration of her college comrades, but at home, she’s seen as an idealistic naif — mocked, in particular, by her older brother Milan (Miodrag Dragicevic), who is staunchly right-wing in his sympathies.

Milan’s similarly inclined friends join in the teasing, but one does so with a little less gusto: 22-year-old Stefan (Andrija Krivokapić) is a working-class punk who goes with the flow of his social group, but doesn’t seem wholehearted in his pro-government stance. Perhaps sensing his lack of commitment, Lena taunts him back. This hint of connection between them is later made concrete when, at the demonstration, the two are complicit in an act of defiance — throwing a cobblestone at a policeman, badly injuring him — and must skip town for the night.

As they flee, their mutual attraction deepens, but they must also parse their political differences. There’s no great capitulation or come-to-Jesus moment here, however. “Until the Day Ends” isn’t an outright romance, or a tale of a proud, gathering storm of resistance; rather, it finds human emotions and obligations sometimes messily at odds with social and political ideals.

Narratively, the momentum crests at the protest, abetted by Maksimović’s most dynamic cinematic trickery — which extends to a shot from the perspective of the errant, offending stone. As a more intimate two-hander in the second half, the film is less urgent, but kept compelling by the push-pull chemistry between its two punchy young leads, playing characters who are alike in their combative vulnerability, but little more than that. Trifunović, in particular, is a real find, unpredictable in her coiled-up physicality and alternately commanding and petulant presence. Lena bristles with angry, frustrated optimism, recognizable to anyone who has ever, at one point or another, felt alone in trying to change the world.

article_text:
This week and next, we’re handing over The Film Comment Podcast to the participants of the 2026 Film at Lincoln Center Critics Academy —an annual program for up-and-coming critics held during the New York Film Festival, led by Film Comment editors.

For this week’s episode, four of this year’s critics—Yezen Saadah, Kathy Ou, Samuel Brodsky, and Rebecca Turner — discuss some of their highlights from the shorts screening as part of NYFF’s Currents Program 5: The Material Ghost , including Peggy Ahwesh’s The Wayfinders , Adam Piron’s The Flesh of the Mountain , and Kevin Jerome Everson’s National Seating .

"translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我驻足在《悬浮》前凝视了半小时之久。近看时，赫尔画作中的图层似乎彼此独立——它们相互叠加，却没有发生完全的交互。然而，若从合适的距离看去，这些富有节奏感的元素便会凝聚成一个令人慰藉的视觉谜题。填满画布的正交线条让人感觉仿佛有一排微小的刀片正在切入我的视线。画作的每一半都似乎是一个静静地与另一半相矛盾的完整宇宙。随着时间推移，个别的圆点开始从人群中脱颖而出。", "translated": article_text:
The grid in the artist’s hands becomes a paradoxical thing: highly regimented yet somehow entropic

A grid is a simple framework with radical implications. Its neat subdivisions offer a means of imposing order, yet its endlessly repeatable pattern conjures the very sense of boundlessness it seeks to contain. In her show Annunciation at Greene Naftali, Hanna Hur utilises this paradoxical quality of the grid to create a suite of hypnotic paintings whose power comes from her ability to instigate a feedback loop between several overlapping layers. Hur’s compositional elements are highly regimented. Ruler-straight orthogonal lines of coloured pencil appear in every work, and each layer is ruthlessly concise. Together these interlocking motifs reverberate with radiant detail.

Hur’s paintings are strongest when the clarity of their graphic structures accentuate the entropic qualities of liquid paint. In Suspension (all works 2026), a nearly-four-metre diptych, coin-size circles of white and pearlescent pigment are painted over each intersection of an underlying grid, punctuating these spatial intervals with a shimmering full stop. Over this matrix Hur has brushed a thin veil of lapis lazuli pigment in short vertical strokes. The mineral blue settles unevenly across its surface like a glowing azure sediment. Underneath these layers a blurred chequerboard pattern of watery black horizontal brush marks over gesso creates a churning sensation, giving the work a pulse.

I remain transfixed in front of Suspension for half an hour. Up close, the layers in Hur’s paintings seem to sit independently of one another – superimposed without fully interacting. From the right distance, however, these rhythmic elements cohere into a soothing visual puzzle. The orthogonal lines that fill the canvas come to feel like an array of tiny blades slicing into my gaze. Each half of the painting seems to be a complete cosmos quietly contradicting its counterpart. Over time, individual dots begin to distinguish themselves from the crowd.

Hur’s concision offers a rare reprieve from a cultural landscape that is loud, performative and oversaturated. In her pulsating grids, this economy feels effortless; in her figurative works, however, it is less convincing. Two paintings in the show, both titled Auto Annunciate , feature the silhouette of a cloaked figure with open hands – based on, according to the exhibition text, Antonello da Messina’s Virgin Annunciate (c. 1475). The line that articulates Mary’s hands looks oversimplified and cartoonish, diminishing the impact of the implied protagonist whose outline occupies much of the canvas. Even the enchanting lapis lazuli haze underperforms in these works because its edges feel hesitant and imprecise as it attempts to capture the curve of the Madonna’s cloak. Here, the effort to signify undoes the impact of the symbolic figure, breaking the spell of the painting.

By contrast, the diptych Angel xvi features a spinelike pattern at the seam between its two panels. Composed of partial circles and horizontal bars, the pattern made me acutely aware of the vertebrae holding up my torso. Because Hur uses thinned paint, drawn lines and raw pigments without added binder, the paintings’ surfaces lack body in terms of obvious texture or lustre. This absence builds tension with the body of the viewer and the edges of the canvas. In the quasi-figurative works, this tension becomes the distinction between bodily sensation and the visual signs through which a body is represented. In a sense, between feeling and thinking – an impossible choice.

Hanna Hur: Annunciation is at Greene Naftali, New York, 10 September – 31 October

article_text:
東京で見るアフリカ現代美術の「いま」──豊田通商のアートアワード初代受賞者5人の作品展が開催

アフリカ の現代美術を世界に発信する「THE TOYOTA TSUSHO CFAO African Art Award」の受賞者5人を紹介する展覧会が、 東京 の2会場で開催される。各地のアートシーンを担う作家の作品が集い、本人たちが創作の背景を語るトークも行われる。

豊田通商とグループ会社のCFAO SASは2025年夏、 アフリカ の現代美術を世界に発信する新たなアートアワード「THE TOYOTA TSUSHO CFAO African Art Award」を創設した。現地で活動するアーティストの継続的な支援と、国際的な活躍の機会拡大を目指す同アワードの第1回受賞者5人の作品を紹介する展覧会が、 東京 の2会場で開催される（space Unで10月23日から31日まで、銀座 蔦屋書店で10月30日から11月3日まで）。

第1回の最優秀賞を受賞したのは、ジンバブエのモファット・タカディワ（Moffat Takadiwa）。優秀賞にはコンゴ民主共和国のゴゼット・ルボンド（Gosette Lubondo）と南アフリカのウナティ・ムコント（Unathi Mkonto）、スポンサー賞にはボツワナのカトレゴ・C・L・トワラ（Katlego C.L. Twala）とエチオピアのティズタ・ベルハヌ（Tizta Berhanu）が選ばれた。

選考にあたっては、世界各地で活躍するキュレーターや評論家などの美術関係者35人が、アフリカ54カ国のアートシーンを代表する約100人のアーティストを推薦。その中から、 カルティエ 現代美術財団マネージングディレクターのクリス・デルコン、 パレ・ド・トーキョー 館長のギヨーム・デザンジュ、キュレーターの 長谷川祐子 、黒澤浩美らで構成される国際審査員が選出した受賞者5人が、2026年3月に発表された。受賞者には賞金のほか、世界3カ国で作品を展示する機会が設けられている。今年6月のトーゴでの展示に続き、10月には東京展、2027年4月にはフランスでの展示が予定されている。

東京展の開幕に合わせ、space Unでは10月23日17時からオープニングレセプションが開かれる。豊田通商の担当者とspace Unディレクターの中谷尚生が登壇し、本プロジェクトの背景やアフリカの現代美術をめぐる今後の展望について対談する。

また、10月31日15時30分からは、同会場に受賞アーティスト5人が集まり、それぞれの制作活動や作品に込めた思い、創作の背景を語る。キュレーターのキャサリン・ゴフォーと、国際審査員を務めた黒澤浩美も参加し、アフリカの現代美術を取り巻く環境や国際的な文化交流の可能性、次世代のアーティストの未来について意見を交わす。

article_text:
Museum de Fundatie in the Netherlands invites applications for a Curator of Contemporary Art to develop exhibitions, expand art-historical perspectives and engage diverse audiences across its locations in Zwolle and Heino.

Open Call:

Museum de Fundatie is recruiting a Curator of Contemporary Art with broad art-historical knowledge, an international outlook and an interest in exploring new approaches to contemporary artistic practice.

The appointed curator will contribute to the museum’s exhibition programme, collection research and publications, developing projects that connect artists, ideas and audiences. The position calls for an experienced professional who can combine independent research with collaborative exhibition-making, translating critical perspectives into accessible and engaging presentations. Particular emphasis is placed on knowledge of artistic practices beyond Europe and the United States, along with an understanding of contemporary developments in the international art world.

Institutional Context:

Museum de Fundatie is an art museum in the Netherlands, operating across two locations: Museum de Fundatie in Zwolle and Kasteel het Nijenhuis in Heino.

Its collection comprises more than 16,000 objects, spanning the late Middle Ages to the present and representing artistic traditions from different parts of the world. Through exhibitions, public programmes, education and research, the museum seeks to make art accessible to broad audiences while encouraging critical engagement with contemporary society.

The institution is examining its future direction through questions of representation, accessibility and the relationship between local histories and international artistic perspectives. The collection remains central to this process, providing a foundation for new research, exhibitions and approaches to interpretation.

Eligibility and Criteria :

Applicants must demonstrate substantial knowledge of contemporary art, strong research capabilities and experience in curatorial practice.

Essential requirements include:

A completed academic degree in art history, at least at master’s level.

A minimum of three years of relevant professional experience as a curator or in a comparable role within the museum or arts sector.

Demonstrable experience in art-historical research and developing exhibitions and publications.

Knowledge of contemporary artistic practices beyond Europe and the United States.

The ability to translate research and ideas into engaging exhibitions, texts and audience-focused presentations.

Strong organisational and communication skills, including experience managing projects, budgets and deadlines.

Ability to initiate projects independently while collaborating with colleagues, artists, researchers, and external partners.

An established national or international professional network, or the capacity and ambition to develop one.

Excellent written and spoken English, basic Dutch communication skills and a willingness to improve Dutch proficiency.

The museum seeks a curator who approaches art history critically, demonstrates intellectual curiosity and is willing to experiment with new perspectives.

Museum de Fundatie encourages applications regardless of background, age, gender, religion, neurodiversity or disability.

Evaluation Process:

Museum de Fundatie will review applications, and shortlisted candidates will be invited to interviews scheduled for 11 and 17 December 2026.

The published vacancy does not specify the selection committee’s composition or a detailed assessment framework.

Candidates should show how their experience, research interests, and curatorial approach align with the museum’s commitment to artistic enquiry, collaboration, and accessibility.

Practical Information:

Position: Curator of Contemporary Art

Institution: Museum de Fundatie

Location: Zwolle and Heino, the Netherlands

Working hours: 36 hours per week

Application deadline: 29 November 2026

Interview dates: 11 and 17 December 2026

Contract: Initial one-year appointment, with the possibility of extension and permanent employment.

Salary: Scale 11 of the Dutch Museum Collective Labour Agreement (Museum-cao), depending on qualifications and experience.

The position offers an opportunity to work with the museum’s collection of more than 16,000 objects, collaborate with an established team and contribute to exhibitions and research across its two locations.

Applications and Queries:

Application deadline: 29 November 2026 .

Candidates are required to submit:

A curriculum vitae (CV).

A motivation letter.

Submit both documents in PDF format.

Send applications to: vacature@museumdefundatie.nl

For the attention of: Beatrice von Bormann, Managing Director.

Official vacancy information: https://museumdefundatie.nl/en/about-museum/work-us

Please direct questions about the position to the same email address.

OA0416，1985），以及马里奥·加西亚·托雷斯（Mario García Torres）和米罗斯瓦夫·巴尔卡（Mirosław Bałka）的几件后观念主义手势作品。这里还有一组达亚尼塔·辛格（Dayanita Singh）的派对照片，以及索米亚·桑卡尔·博斯（Soumya Sankar Bose）和乔·拉特克利夫（Jo article_text:
The 2003-founded troupe’s theatre productions are a site on which fiction and reality are constantly confused – and so too in the gallery

Lagartijas Tiradas al Sol (Lizards laying in the sun)’s vision of theatre involves sparse scenography (more honest than it is minimalistic), a bold juxtaposition of the historical with the confessional and a preference for exposition over dialogue in their dramaturgy. The 2003-founded troupe’s theatre productions are a site on which fiction and reality are constantly confused, much like they are in life.

The group exhibition No es un poema, aunque soñemos muchas cosas (It’s not a poem, even if we dream of many things), is Lagartijas Tiradas al Sol’s second curatorial endeavour and is full of effective gestures: warm lights that dim up and down cyclically over walls covered with brown paper and plastic sheeting, among plants, some bricks and a modest fishtank. It feels simultaneously staged and lived in, unfussy yet focused. My eye kept wandering to an old metal fan affixed near the back wall, with pretty ribbons lazily dangling from its shield. The show includes works by 17 artists, alongside videos and props used in previous Lagartijas plays. There is an immense, entrancingly braided textile by Olga de Amaral ( FIBRAS REF. OA0416 , 1985), as well as a couple of postconceptual gestures by Mario García Torres and Mirosław Bałka. There is a nice group of party photos by Dayanita Singh and politically tinted landscape photography by Soumya Sankar Bose and Jo Ratfcliffe; as well as a landscape painting by Matthew Krishanu right behind a massive (mountainscape) backdrop by Pedro Pizarro that divides the room.

The works by the father and son Eduardo and Pedro Pizarro, although different, extend affective tendrils towards each other. The first creates baroque religious paintings; the second frescoes and backdrops for Lagartijas. A painting by Eduardo opens the show, the slightly amateurish but charming Inmaculada concepción (2016) hung over a striking cascade of golden cellophane (previously a background for one of the Lagartijas plays), evoking the excesses of gilded churrigueresco churches. Pedro is represented by a number of works, including a sombre and beautiful quartet of paintings, Nadie hereda el cansancio (No one inherits exhaustion, 2026), representing, in earthy colours, the funeral rites of the inhabitants of Yanhuitlán, a town in the mountains of Oaxaca that has been virtually abandoned by the young but where the elderly remain to till the land. Both Pedro and Lagartijas Tiradas al Sol cofounder Luisa Pardo live there now, pursuing pedagogical projects around art, architecture and theatre for the children who remain.

Pardo’s arrival in the Mixteca Alta, as the region is known, over a decade ago, was the subject of the play Epifanía sideral (Sidereal epiphany, 2026), a fragment of which is presented upstairs in a second gallery. The small stage contains only a table to the side, a chair with some books and a cloud of crumpled plastic at its centre. From the cloud hang plastic bags filled with water, which are, at one point, pierced by Pardo with her teeth to signal rain (the water subsequently flows into a series of zinc tubs). In terms of the narrative aspects of her performance, Pardo braids fiction and confession into a story of her arrival, as a self-described “predictable, comfortable, urban” dweller, in a land that was very much not her own. She was welcomed with warmth by a family of women, and with scepticism from townspeople sick of having their experiences extracted for academic research – “I am not an academic”, Pardo repeats to herself in a work that, perhaps inadvertently, also highlights some of the issues attending ‘research-based’ art practices, as well as the issues of bringing art and life together (which is another subtheme of the show as a whole).

The performance and the exhibition collectively form a well-rounded, critical and ambitious project. One that can, however, be a little repetitive in its focus on landscape (and related themes, which have almost become clichés, of ‘territory’ and ‘conflict’) in works of decidedly uneven quality. At its best, however, the artworks play with an obvious theatricality to evoke a narrative that, like the stories Lagartijas are invested in telling, is not necessarily complete or predetermined, but rather quilted together from different aspects of a fragmented reality.

No es un poema, aunque soñemos muchas cosas at Galerie Nordenhake, Mexico City, 3 September – 24 October

article_text:
The photography of Chardchakaj Waikawee, born in Bangkok in 1980, resists easy classification. It belongs neither to social documentary, with its cool rigor, nor to art portraiture, with its aestheticizing restraint. It is something else, something harder to name, and therefore more precious. His work has traveled internationally for more than fifteen years. “Youth”, the exhibition devoted to him by London’s Graces Mews, brings together a body of analog photographs taken between 2008 and 2020.

The title borrows the Thai phrase wai run , a term that reaches far beyond its literal translation to describe an inner disposition, an energy of being that neither age nor poverty can extinguish. Waikawee’s subjects include motorcycle-taxi drivers, street vendors, and more broadly the young people who survive on the margins of Bangkok’s economy. “Bangkok is chaos,” he says. “Heaven and hell exist on the same street.”

One enters the exhibition through a filmed portrait of the photographer, his voice continuing to murmur through the galleries like an undertow. This sonic device anchors the images in a meditation on memory, time and value: sober words for photographs that are anything but. For Waikawee’s eye plays as much as it bears witness. One need only look at the boy sipping Coca-Cola from a plastic bag, staring straight into the lens with quiet defiance, to be convinced of it. Or the punk whose extravagant pink mohawk bursts through the open sunroof of a champagne-colored Mercedes.

What strikes one, technically, is the deliberate insolence of the process. Waikawee works with expired film, repaired cameras, hand-printing techniques. Cross-processing produces unpredictable chromatic shifts — lemon yellow, scorched orange, acid magenta — which the photographer treats as so many traces of time’s passage upon the material itself. The scratches, the dust, the chemical marks are not accidents but the visible memory of the making, a reminder that every image is also a physical object.

Full of life, these portraits are anything but miserabilist. “Each image reflects a relationship before it becomes a photograph,” Waikawee notes. He foregrounds the personality, the friendship, the singular sense of style of his subjects, who wear their appearance as armor against the social and economic invisibility the city imposes upon them.

Take the laborers crammed into the back of a truck, riding home at night in a tableau at once baroque and entirely ordinary. Or the boy whose back, tattooed with sacred Sak Yant script, is covered in inscriptions down to the waistband of his jeans. One will long remember, too, the doll-like face of the young woman, her eyes lined in black, holding the camera’s gaze without flinching. So many ways, for this sidelined but defiant youth, to compose, with whatever means are to hand, a presence in the world.

“Youth” , by Chardchakaj Waikawee, runs until 19 September 2026 at Graces Mews , London.

article_text:
Sundance Film Festival 2027 has announced its first lineup for the inaugural Boulder, Colorado edition with the The Legacy Program, formerly known as From the Collection, which includes archival and restored screenings of indie classics that launched at the fest.

Cinephile social platform, Letterboxd, is a co-presenter of the Legacy program, and there will be forthcoming details for onsite activations at the Boulder cinema event which takes place Jan. 21-31. The Legacy portion of Sundance will occur during the fest’s second half from Tuesday, Jan. 27-Sunday, Jan. 31.

There will still be an online portion of the festival, which will run from Thursday, Jan. 28-Sunday, Jan. 31.

The Legacy lineup includes the 2002 Sundance Film Festival version of Better Luck Tomorrow (Justin Lin); a digital 4K restoration of Dogtown and Z-Boys (Stacy Peralta); a 35th anniversary screening of Fool’s Fire (Julie Taymor); Nitrate Kisses (Barbara Hammer), which premiered in the U.S. at the Festival 35 years ago and whose director is at the center of Brydie O’Connor’s 2026 Sundance Film Festival documentary Barbara Forever ; a 25th anniversary screening of Real Women Have Curves (Patricia Cardoso); a 35th anniversary screening of Swoon (Tom Kalin); and a 25th anniversary screening of a 4K restoration of Y tu mamá también (Alfonso Cuarón).

Watch on Deadline

The Legacy program will also include a two-part session on the final weekend of the Festival called “Sundance Film Festival presents: Cinema Interruptus featuring Memento ” (Christopher Nolan), featuring a 4K restoration and discussion. Legacy screenings will include director appearances and select cast members in attendance, Next reps the 30th anniversary of Sundance Institute and the UCLA Film & Television Archive. Together they established a film preservation initiative, the Sundance Institute Collection at UCLA, to ensure the long-term preservation of independent film. The Collection currently holds material from over 1,000 titles and has participated in restorations of Hoop Dreams , River of Grass , Mysterious Skin , Doom Generation , Just Another Girl on the IRT , High Art , Go Fish , Three Seasons , Paris Is Burning , Superstar , Unzipped , The Hours and Times , SLAM , and, this year, Better Luck Tomorrow and Swoon . “We’re excited to kick off the Festival season in earnest with this first 2027 Sundance Film Festival announcement, revealing some of our Legacy programming,” said Eugene Hernandez, Director, Sundance Film Festival and Public Programming. “Each year we honor the legacy of our founder Robert Redford and the history of the Sundance Film Festival by looking back at just a few of the films and filmmakers who have shaped our history. Our first festival in our new home in Boulder, Colorado will bring change, but as we evolve, we’ll keep at our core what we celebrate: our rich history. Sundance will always uplift independent voices, and our Legacy slate is a beautiful example of that. We are also pleased to announce Letterboxd’s co-partnership for the Legacy category — it’s great to collaborate with organizations that build momentum and excitement for a culture of cinematic discovery, and we look forward to having them at the Festival with us in January.”

“Revisiting and becoming newly acquainted with films from our previous lineups in a theatrical setting, in community, and with some of the talent behind the films is a rare treat — even more so when these projects have been restored,” said Kim Yutani, Director of Programming, Sundance Film Festival.

“We’re really looking forward to welcoming back these artists and know that audiences will enjoy the opportunity to complement the new films we will soon be announcing with these classics.”

“Our Legacy programming at the Sundance Film Festival grew out of a partnership with the UCLA Film & Television Archive and its continued growth is running in parallel to the incredible moment repertory cinema is having across the country right now,” said John Nein, Sundance Film Festival Senior Programmer and Director of Strategic Initiatives. “This program offers a space for brand-new restorations of classic independent films to be discovered or rediscovered by audiences as the creative teams behind these films reunite — it’s an exciting way of celebrating what these artists have brought to independent storytelling.”

Below are descriptions of the Legacy lineup: 25th Anniversary of Better Luck Tomorrow / U.S.A. (Director, Screenwriter, and Producer: Justin Lin, Screenwriters: Ernesto Foronda, Fabian Marquez, Producers: Julie Asato, Ernesto Foronda) — To escape the crushing pressure of academic perfection, a group of high-achieving teens lead a secret, thrill-seeking double life of petty crime that quickly spins out of control. Cast: Karin Anna Cheung, John Cho, Roger Fan, Sung Kang, Parry Shen, Jason Tobin. Fiction. Better Luck Tomorrow premiered at the 2002 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Dramatic Competition. It was subsequently released with small changes in the edit. The original 2002 Sundance Film Festival cut of Better Luck Tomorrow was restored by the UCLA Film & Television Archive in collaboration with Sundance Institute and Perfect Storm Entertainment, with funding provided by Chris Quintos Cathcart, co-CEO of Unapologetic Projects. The 4K restoration utilized the original 35 mm camera negatives, 35 mm Sundance Film Festival print, and DA-88 sound materials and was supervised by filmmaker Justin Lin at Resillion and Deluxe Audio Services. Additional lab services by Roundabout Entertainment, Inc. The release version has also been restored and archived. Special thanks to Paramount Pictures for permission to screen the film.

25th Anniversary of Dogtown and Z-Boys / U.S.A (Director and Screenwriter: Stacy Peralta, Screenwriter: Craig Stecyk, Producer: Agi Orsi) — The Z-Boys: outcast surf rats from the run-down Dogtown neighborhood in Venice, California, who revolutionized skateboarding with their innovative style and attitude. The documentary is an exploration of the birth of a cultural phenomenon, narrated by Sean Penn and featuring old-school skating footage, a blistering soundtrack, and interviews with Tony Alva, Jay Adams, and Tony Hawk. Dogtown and Z-Boys premiered at the 2001 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Documentary Competition and won the Audience Award: Documentary and Directing Award: Documentary. 2027 marks the 25th anniversary of its theatrical release. The 4K digital restoration was undertaken from the original 35 mm elements by Sony Pictures Classics. The restoration was approved by the filmmakers. 35th Anniversary of Fool’s Fire / U.S.A. (Director, Screenwriter, and Producer: Julie Taymor, Producer: Kerry Orent) — A captured dwarf, Hopfrog, is forced to become jester to a tyrannical king. But when the King is gifted with another little person, whom the king debases and shames, Hopfrog plots a terrible revenge. Based on the story “Hop-Frog” by Edgar Allan Poe. Cast: Michael J. Anderson, Tom Hewitt, Mireille Mossé. Fiction. Fool’s Fire premiered at the 1992 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Dramatic Competition. This new restoration was created by the nonprofit IndieCollect in collaboration with Julie Taymor and with support from the Golden Globe Foundation, using a 6.5K scan of the original 35 mm negative and a soundtrack restored by Endpoint Audio Labs from the optical track negative. Featuring an extended conversation with Julie Taymor and clips from The Making of Fool’s Fire , exploring the film’s artistry and cutting-edge use of high definition.

Nitrate Kisses / U.S.A. (Director: Barbara Hammer) — A portrait of queer sexuality that weaves striking images of four lesbian and gay couples with archival footage, interviews, sexual imagery, and queer cinema dating back to the 1930s to unearth forbidden and long-invisible histories. Documentary. Nitrate Kisses had its U.S. premiere at the 1993 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Documentary Competition. Nitrate Kisses was preserved by the Academy Film Archive. The original 16 mm A/B-rolls were scanned at 4K and restored by BB Optics. The mono mix was digitized from the original 16 mm mag track. The restoration was funded by Frameline and supervised by The Estate of Barbara Hammer and Brydie O’Connor. The 25th Anniversary of Real Women Have Curves / U.S.A. (Director: Patricia Cardoso, Screenwriters: George LaVoo, Josefina López, Producers: George Lavoo, Effie Brown) — Ana, a first-generation Mexican American teenager, fights for her independence and her curves in a war of wills with her mother. Based on the play by Josefina López. Cast: America Ferrera, George Lopez, Ingrid Oliu, Lupe Ontiveros, Brian Sites. Real Women Have Curves premiered at the 2002 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Dramatic Competition and took home the Audience Award: Dramatic and the Special Jury Prize for Acting for America Ferrera and Lupe Ontiveros. Supervised by director Patricia Cardoso and director of photography Jim Denault, this new 4K restoration was undertaken by Criterion in collaboration with Warner Bros. Pictures, Sundance Institute, and the Academy Film Archive from the 35 mm original camera negative. The 35th Anniversary of Swoon / U.S.A. (Director and Screenwriter: Tom Kalin, Producers: Christine Vachon) — The true story of Nathan Leopold and Richard Loeb, who kidnapped and brutally murdered 14-year-old Bobby Franks in Chicago in 1924. The revelation that these wealthy Jewish college students had a sexual relationship scandalized the nation. After their arrest and trial, they were sentenced to life plus 99 years. Cast: Craig Chester, Michael Kirby, John A. Mudd, Daniel Schlachet, Natalie Stanford, Michael Stumm, Ron Vawter. Swoon premiered at the 1992 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Dramatic Competition and took home the Excellence in Cinematography Award: Dramatic. Swoon was restored by the Academy Film Archive and UCLA Film & Television Archive in collaboration with Frameline, Strand Releasing, and Sundance Institute in 4K from the original 16 mm A/B camera negatives, 35 mm interpositive, 35 mm dupe negative, and 35 mm magnetic track. The restoration was supervised by Tom Kalin and Ellen Kuras at Roundabout Entertainment, Inc. and Deluxe Audio Services. Restoration funding was provided by the Academy Film Archive and UCLA Film & Television Archive with additional support from Frameline, Ellen Kuras, Strand Releasing, and Sundance Institute.

The 25th Anniversary of Y tu mamá también / Mexico (Director, Screenwriter and Producer: Alfonso Cuarón, Screenwriter: Carlos Cuarón, Producer: Jorge Vergara) — After their girlfriends jet off for the summer, a pair of Mexico City teenagers become bewitched by an older Spanish woman they meet at a wedding. When she agrees to accompany them on a road trip, the three form an increasingly intense and sensual bond. Cast: Gael García Bernal, Diego Luna, Maribel Verdú. Y tu mamá también screened at the 2002 Sundance Film Festival as part of the Special Events category. Newly restored by Esperanto Films in 4K under the supervision of filmmaker Alfonso Cuarón and cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki. The feature is a Janus Films release.

LEGACY SPECIAL EVENTS Memento / U.S.A. (Director: Christopher Nolan) — A former insurance investigator who now suffers from anterograde amnesia uses notes and tattoos to hunt down his wife’s murderer. Fiction. Memento had its U.S. festival premiere at the 2001 Sundance Film Festival in the U.S. Dramatic Competition and it took home the Waldo Salt Screenwriting Award. Restored in 4K from original interpositive materials by Umbrella with approval from director Christopher Nolan. Cinema Interruptus is also part of our Offscreen program, to be announced in its entirety soon.

As part of the screening, there will be Sundance Film Festival presents: Cinema Interruptus featuring Memento . A tradition first established by the late Roger Ebert, Cinema Interruptus is communal film criticism in two sessions. As Memento screens, participants can yell “Stop!” at any point to make a comment or ask a question, after which the film will resume. Critic and author Josh Larsen — who hosted Interruptus at the University of Colorado Boulder’s Conference on World Affairs from 2017 to 2024 — will moderate the discussion, with the goal of finishing the entire movie by the end of the second session.

article_text:
Billionaire collector William “Bill” Koch is ready to sell more of his art. After parting ways with $84 million worth of American art at Christie’s in January, he’s putting another group of paintings up for sale this November, including works by Claude Monet and Paul Cézanne that could fetch as much as $18 million apiece.

Christie’s said the collection, which also includes works by Edgar Degas, Henri Matisse, Joan Miró, and Diego Rivera, is expected to bring more than $40 million during its marquee sales in New York next month.

The announcement marks the latest chapter in what has become a very lucrative relationship between Koch and the auction house. In June 2025, Christie’s sold $28.8 million worth of wine from his cellar , followed by his Western American art auction seven months later. Both sales exceeded expectations, according to Christie’s.

And it isn’t just art and wine that Koch has been selling. He’s also been trying to find a buyer for Elk Mountain Lodge, his sprawling 52-acre estate in Aspen, Colorado. The property went on the market in January 2025 for $125 million, but after failing to attract a buyer, Koch slashed the asking price to $99 million and put it up for auction in July. The estate, which he bought for $26.5 million in 2007, includes a 16,631-square-foot main house, seven guest cabins, and enough amenities to make leaving the property seem almost unnecessary.

It’s unclear what’s behind Koch’s motivation to sell. In under two years, the 85-year-old has parted with more than $112 million in art and wine, with another $40 million or more potentially coming next month. While it certainly looks like the billionaire is doing some serious housecleaning, Christie’s hasn’t offered an explanation, and Koch hasn’t publicly connected the sales to any broader plans, though in the release Koch says that he hopes “art lovers around the world can take the same enjoyment as I have, in collecting these works my hope is that collectors will find something that speaks to their passion and that they are able to share it with their friends and loved ones.”

For the upcoming sale, Koch is turning his attention to European and Latin American art. Leading the group is Monet’s Champ d’avoine et coquelicots (1890), a landscape depicting a field of oats and poppies near the artist’s home in Giverny, France. Koch bought the painting in 1985, and the work carries an estimate of $12 million to $18 million.

Sharing top billing is Cézanne’s Tasse, verre et fruits , a still life painted around 1877 that features apples, a cup, and a glass arranged on a tabletop. Koch acquired the painting in 1986, and Christie’s has given it the same $12 million to $18 million estimate. Both paintings will appear in the house’s 20th Century Evening Sale.

Another highlight is Matisse’s Jeune femme fardée à l’orientale (La bayadère) , a 1929 painting of a nude inspired by the classical ballet La Bayadère . It’s expected to bring between $5 million and $7 million.

A Degas work, Scène de ballet , is estimated at $3 million to $5 million. The pastel over monotype has a particularly interesting history: it was originally purchased directly from Degas by Philadelphia collector Annie Riddle Scott on the advice of Impressionist painter Mary Cassatt. (Another impression of the underlying monotype belongs to the Clark Art Institute in Williamstown, Massachusetts.)

Koch’s collection also includes Rivera’s Vendedora de flores en Xochimilco (1929) and Miró’s Peinture (1950), each estimated at $2.5 million to $3.5 million. A 1971 Chagall painting, Danseuse à la robe fleurie , carries a $1.2 million to $1.8 million estimate, while Gabriele Münter’s Kind mit Puppe (1909) is expected to bring between $900,000 and $1.2 million.

Koch, an industrialist, America’s Cup winner, and longtime collector, has spent decades assembling collections that range from fine art to rare wines. “I feel very fortunate that with hard work, business success, and a great deal of luck, I have been able to collect things that resonate with me,” Koch said in a statement. “The masterpieces in this sale are among my favorites.”

The works will be spread across Christie’s 20th Century Evening Sale, Impressionist and Modern Art Day Sale, and Works on Paper Sale during the house’s November marquee week in New York.
